explanation: Fires on a token in the middle of a predictable multi-token name or term, where the earlier pieces strongly predict the rest: UNIT[ED] STATES, isoflur[ane], ion [thr]usters, rab[5], Qt [Quick], 'powers that [be]', page[-footer], schemas[.android]. The context makes the completion obvious, and there is no single shared topic. Weak on ordinary function words and commas.

Fires on a gerund or present participle ending in -ing (or its -ing subword) used as a noun or noun modifier, especially after a determiner or preposition: 'the [powering] mechanism', 'the [sealing] element', 'taxi[ing]', 'for[aging] bee', 'punch[ing] bag'. It is moderate for -ing nominals like mining or texting, and weak on non -ing words.

No clear common feature. Top examples mix name completions (K[immel], Fukuy[ama], Dop[pler]), 'coming [to]', set phrases ('easier [said]', 'Big [Ten]', 'Bay [State]', 'registered [office]') and code tokens. All seem to be tokens that complete a highly predictable continuation, but that is too broad to tell what fires and what does not.

Fires on the assignment or definition operator right after a variable name in math or code, mostly '=' or 'be' in 'Let f =' / 'Let b be', '$A =', 'var max =' (strongest). It also fires on nearby math-structure tokens such as LaTeX '{', '\left(' and '\leq', and weakly on some prose function words.

Fires on the line break (often '.\n') that ends a title or heading line and comes before the body text, most typically the period plus newline after a paper title in an abstract ('...in heart failure[.\n]We hypothesized'). Ordinary sentence-ending periods and newlines get weaker activation.

Fires on a token that completes or extends a short noun phrase whose fill is predictable from context: the second half of an acronym in parentheses (CR[RT], ES[RD], MD[R]), weight-class or category words (fly[weight], 'mini flyweight [division]', 'Adult Standards [format]'), idiom pieces ('pound [of]', 'in [part]', 'half-empty or [half]'), plus some commas. The behavior is diffuse but leans toward predictable phrase completion.

Fires mainly on '#' in LaTeX/markdown section labels of the form 'Introduction {#sec...}', at about 83% very consistently. Its other top activations (e.g. 'At some [point]', 'ChallengePassword[:]', '#[doc [=]') are scattered tokens that open a label or value.

Fires on word-initial tokens that start with 'U'/'Ul'/'Un', usually capitalized and at the start of a name or word: Ul(rik), Ul(m), Ul(tron), Ul(trasound), Un(ivar), UN(ABLE), U(ppsala), U(ML), U(WP). Lowercase 'ul'/'un' word-starts (ultras, ultracold, ultimately) also fire. Weaker on 'under' and other u-words.

Fires on verbs of telling, giving, showing or helping that take a recipient, especially in requests or help contexts: 'Can anyone [tell]', 'it [gives] a reading', 'I'll [show] you', 'did not [help] me', 'This [tells] us'. Similar verb slots in other languages fire too. Weaker on other verbs and prepositions.

Fires on names of software developer tools and IDEs and on command-line context: IntelliJ [IDEA], [git], TortoiseSV[N], Grad[le], AutoCAD, swagger, 'File | Settings [|]', and a code-fence opener before a command. Also moderate on 'used [to]/[for]' after describing a tool or instrument.

Fires on 'considered' in passive or classification constructions ('X is [considered]...') and on the same slot filled by related verbs and particles: 'deemed', 'regard [as]', 'seen [as]', 'consider [ourselves]'. Weaker on 'called' and 'referred to [as]'/'known [as]' naming constructions.

Fires on a clause linker right after a noun phrase or clause that starts a relative or subordinate clause: relative pronouns 'which', 'who', 'where', and 'so that', 'if', plus clause-joining ', and' after a comma. 'which' after a plural noun is strongest. Mid and weak examples are scattered.

No single clear feature. Top examples include statistics notation ('+/- [SE]', '+/-', '(+[/-]'), nouns in biomedical titles and phrases (outcome, cases, revision, experience, injury), and assorted function words and code tokens. Possibly a nominal head or completion token in scientific text, but the examples are a mixture.

Mixed. It fires on digits in code identifiers after a repeated variable name (sub[2], stamp[2]), on math operators and commas inside formulas or number lists, and on assorted prose tokens (in, still, to, 's). There is no clear shared trigger beyond tokens that continue a parallel or repeated structure.

Fires on the first subword token of a longer, often technical or medical, word that is split into pieces: h[exam]ethyl, [cr]adles, [dev]otions, [pem]phigus, [te]ats, [par]affin, [polym]orphonuclear, [per]icardium, [att]ested. The unit responds to a word-start fragment that needs a continuation, regardless of meaning.

No coherent pattern. Top examples include 'Type [I] error', hypoth[al]amic, ssh[-key]gen, '[http', 'below [normal]', '[proportional] representation', 'Copyright ©', version-number dots and medical subwords. All are tokens inside fixed technical terms, but they come from many unrelated domains.

Mixed. It fires on tokens in non-Latin scripts (Devanagari, Japanese), on 'The' in copyright and project-author headers ('Copyright 1995-2018 [The] OpenSSL Project Authors'), on 'the' in idioms like 'on [the] path/verge', and on code punctuation such as module path '/' and '='. These do not form a single job.

Mixed. It fires on 'IT' completing 'CIRCU[IT]' in US court-of-appeals headers (a recurring strong case), on Portuguese verb endings, on '=' in 'Let o(r) =' math, on code tokens (method [stub], .org), and on assorted words. There is no unifying trigger beyond completions of fixed strings.

No clear pattern. Top examples range over 'generated [by]', 'University [Press]', '3 [bedrooms]', 'Pay[roll]', code-import path pieces, version and region digits, and adverbs. These look like predictable continuation tokens in boilerplate or list contexts, but they are too varied to predict.

Fires on a '0' digit token inside a run of zeros, especially leading or padding zeros after a decimal point or '0x' ('P < 0.0[0]1', '0x00[0]000', '#00[0]', '+00[0]0', '43,00[0]'). Small offshoots fire on word-final caps pieces (SOPHOM[ORE], OREG[ON]).

No clear pattern. Top examples mix biochemical subwords (deac[etyl]ase), Portuguese suffixes, idiom pieces ('Safe to [say]', 'no [doubt]', 'For [once]', 'move [on]', 'not getting very [far]'), and nouns that complete phrases ('country [chart]', 'civil [society]', 'Morris [Maze]'). Perhaps a token that completes an idiom or collocation, but it is broad.
